title: Centaurus A
caption: The active galaxy Centaurus A, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope, APEX and Chandra
celestial: Centaurus A, NGC 5128 · constellation Centaurus · about 13 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESO/WFI (Optical); MPIfR/ESO/APEX/A.Weiss et al. (Submillimetre); NASA/CXC/CfA/R.Kraft et al. (X-ray)

recognition.text: Ranked #30 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Lobes and jets streaming from the center of this galaxy are revealed in this composite, laid over its stars and its characteristic dust lane shown in close to true color. This is Centaurus A, also known as NGC 5128, about 13 million light-years away, pictured by combining data from three instruments working at very different wavelengths.

Each layer shows something different. Visible light from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope at La Silla, Chile, captures the stars and the galaxy's characteristic dust lane. Submillimeter data at 870 microns, from the LABOCA camera on APEX, appear in orange. Data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, shown in blue, trace X-rays.

The lobes and jets stream out from the galaxy's central black hole, which is what makes Centaurus A an active galaxy. Only the visible-light layer shows the galaxy roughly as an eye would, while the orange and blue layers record light far outside the visible range.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (22.71 x 23.92 arcminutes) and distance (13 million light years), the frame spans roughly 86,000 × 90,000 light-years. Its light set out about 13 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Visible light from the Wide Field Imager shows stars and dust in close to true color. Submillimeter data from LABOCA on APEX are shown in orange and Chandra X-rays in blue.
understand.eye: Submillimeter and X-ray light are both invisible to the eye, so only the visible-light layer resembles what an eye could perceive.
